summary.one_line: A sizeable, fast-growing Indian maker of branded generic agrochemicals and seeds. It has a wide distribution network but no hard moat, thin net margins, heavy working capital and a large pending FMC India acquisition with no funding source disclosed. Its governance record is the main problem: a CBI chargesheet naming the company and two promoters, auditor qualifications, and an NFRA-debarred audit committee chair. The IPO mostly repays debt that tends to come back.
bull_points: Revenue from operations grew from Rs.2,229.93 cr in FY24 to Rs.3,151.97 cr in FY26, about 18.9% a year, while PAT grew about 28.9% a year (S1, S6).
Margins improved structurally: gross margin rose from 31.10% to 38.49% and EBITDA margin from 9.38% to 14.47% between FY24 and FY26 (S1).
Distribution scale is real: 14,717 active distributors at FY26, up from 8,992 at FY24, across 23 states and four union territories, plus 583 domestic product registrations (S1, S10).
Rs.270 cr of the Rs.354.77 cr fresh issue goes to debt repayment, at the company (Rs.247.94 cr) and at subsidiary Saffire Crop Science (Rs.22.06 cr) (S2, S3).
The CCI-cleared purchase of FMC India brings licensed FMC brands, a preferred supply agreement for FMC active ingredients, and preferred access to FMC's India pipeline (S12, S13).
bear_points: A CBI case filed in January 2020 over alleged Foreign Trade Policy 2009-2014 violations names the company, two promoters and one director. The ED has provisionally attached Rs.30.21 cr of fixed deposits (S11, S16).

The auditor has qualified its opinion on a Rs.16.30 cr insurance receivable, flagged material weaknesses in internal controls for FY23 to FY25, and qualified FY23 and FY24 accounts over a Rs.109.42 cr TED refund demand (S16).
Returns are thin: FY26 PAT margin was about 4.56% and ROE 7.94%, against peers such as Dhanuka and Bayer CropScience at about 20-21% RoNW in FY25 (S2, S6, S20).

Working capital is heavy and getting heavier: inventory days rose from 122 (FY24) to 160 (FY26), and operating cash flow fell to about Rs.256 cr in FY26 from about Rs.383 cr in FY25 even as EBITDA rose 44.7% (S6, S23).
China supplied about 42% of raw-material cost in FY26 (S29). The business is 97.48% India and monsoon-dependent (S11).
watch_points: How the $252 million FMC India purchase, expected to close by end-2026, gets funded. One commentary calls it a Rs.2,268 cr unfunded acquisition, against a Rs.355 cr fresh issue (S12, S26, S28).
Whether borrowings stay down after the Rs.270 cr repayment. They fell to Rs.820 cr at March 2026 but rebounded to Rs.952 cr by June 2026 and Rs.962.6 cr by August 2026 (S4, S6).
Discharge applications in the CBI and ED proceedings are pending, and further attachments are possible (S22).
Day-1 subscription figures were not available at the time of writing. The anchor book of Rs.135.96 cr included existing shareholder IFC (S14, S15).

reasoning: Governance is the deciding factor. A CBI chargesheet over wrongful Terminal Excise Duty refunds names the company, two promoters and a director. The ED has attached Rs.30.21 cr of deposits. The auditor has qualified the accounts year after year and found material control weaknesses. The audit committee chair is reportedly under a five-year NFRA audit debarment. Investors are being asked to trust reported numbers whose control environment the auditor itself has questioned (S11, S16, S22).

The money raised does little to change the company. Rs.270 cr repays debt that rebuilds every season: borrowings went from Rs.820 cr in March to Rs.952 cr in June 2026. The roughly Rs.85 cr left over goes to unnamed acquisitions and general purposes. Another Rs.100.71 cr is promoter OFS that raises nothing for the company (S2, S6, S11).

A large, transformational acquisition is pending without disclosed funding. The $252 million FMC India deal dwarfs the fresh issue. Integrating a business FMC itself described as producing very limited EBITDA and needing substantial working capital adds execution and leverage risk that IPO investors cannot yet size (S12, S26, S28).

There is no hard moat. Crystal is mainly a branded-generics formulator that imports about 42% of its raw materials from China. Its advantages are distribution reach, registrations and acquired brands, which listed peers also have. Peers convert these into roughly 20% returns on net worth, against Crystal's roughly 7-8% (S1, S20, S29).

Growth quality is mixed. Revenue and EBITDA grew strongly, but PAT growth (22.4%) lagged EBITDA growth (44.7%) in FY26, operating cash flow fell, and inventory days rose to 160. The growth is being financed partly through the balance sheet rather than generating cash (S6, S23).

What would change the call: closure of the CBI and ED matters or a clean audit opinion, disclosed FMC funding that keeps leverage in check, and two or three seasons of listed results showing cash conversion. Without these, the business is worth tracking but not buying at IPO (S14, S16).

subsections.title: What Crystal makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Crystal Crop Protection was incorporated in 1994 as Jai Bharat Crop Chemical Private Limited and became a public company in 2018 (S11). Its registered office is in Ahmedabad and its corporate office in New Delhi (S11). It sells three things to Indian farmers through distributors. The first is crop protection chemicals: herbicides, fungicides, insecticides and combinations. The second is 'natural crop solutions': bio-stimulants, bio-protectants, plant growth regulators, liquid fertilisers and micronutrients. The third is seeds for field crops, vegetables and flowers (S3, S11).

Revenue comes overwhelmingly from branded products sold in India. In FY25, India generated 97.48% of revenue from operations and international sales only 1.72% (S11). Crop protection and natural solutions made up 81.74% of FY25 revenue. Seeds rose from 12.66% of revenue in FY23 to 17.45% in FY25 (S11). In FY26, seeds were 24.92% of domestic branded revenue and crop protection 75.08% (S1). The shift came through acquisitions, not organic growth: Bayer's cotton, mustard, pearl millet and sorghum hybrid seed business in 2021, and I&B Seeds in October 2024 (S1, S11, S25).

blocks.caption: Revenue mix indicators (per RHP/DRHP summaries)
rows: Crop protection + natural solutions share of revenue
Seeds share of domestic branded revenue
Seeds share of domestic branded revenue
India share of revenue from operations

blocks.text: The jump to 50.45% seeds in Q1 FY27 reflects seasonality. Seeds are sold ahead of the kharif sowing season, so a single quarter should not be read as a run-rate (S1, S5).

The RHP summaries describe six crop protection plants and three seed processing units (S1). The DRHP-based detail lists four formulation units (two in Jammu, one in Sonipat, one in Anand) and two technical (active ingredient) units at Nagpur and Dahej. There is also a technical pilot unit at Sonipat, and land has been bought at Jhagadia, Gujarat, for a new plant (S11). The company's website puts combined formulation capacity at 60,900 MT/KL per year and technical capacity at 6,600 MTPA (S9). Plant-wise capacity utilisation could not be confirmed from the sources available.

items: Formulation plants: Sonipat (Haryana), Jammu (two units), Anand (Gujarat). Combined capacity 60,900 MT/KL per year (S9, S11).
Technical plants: Nagpur and Dahej. Combined capacity 6,600 MTPA. IFC's 2021-22 disclosure said a third active-ingredient plant was being installed at Dahej (S8, S9).
Seed processing: Hyderabad/Telangana and Bengaluru (S9, S11).
R&D: Key Research Development Centre at Sonipat plus nine field research stations (S1, S14).
Greenfield: about 31 acres at Jhagadia, Gujarat, for a plant to make both formulations and technicals, with about Rs.100 cr planned over three years (S31).

blocks.text: IFC rates the business Category A (significant environmental and social risk). It cites handling of hazardous chemicals such as chlorine and bromine at Nagpur and Dahej and possible contamination at older plants (S8). Agrochemical manufacturing carries pollution-control and regulatory risk, and this is a reminder of it.

Supply runs from active ingredients (technicals), partly made in-house and largely bought from China and domestic suppliers, to formulation at the four plants, then to the company's distributors. Raw materials are mostly bought on purchase orders, without long-term contracts with most suppliers (S11, S29). In FY25 the top 10 suppliers provided 39.97% of raw-material purchases, down from 51.49% in FY23. In FY23 a single China-based supplier provided 26.16% (S11). RHP-based reviews put the top-10 share at 38.18% in FY26 and China-sourced material at 41.82% of FY26 raw-material cost (in a 40.79%-49.23% range over three years) and 48.84% in Q1 FY27 (S29). One commentary reports the top-10 share rose to 51.33% in Q1 FY27, led by Hebei Bestar at 16.46%. That figure is unverified against the RHP (S28).

On the customer side the company sells to distributors, not end farmers. It had 14,717 active distributors at FY26, up from 8,992 at FY24, supported by 729 sales and marketing staff in 69 regions (S1). Most distributor relationships have no long-term contract (S1). Credit runs up to 90 days, and up to 180 days on some products (S29). No single customer appears material, so customer concentration is low. The real exposure is to the Indian farm cycle as a whole.

blocks.caption: Concentration snapshot
rows: China-sourced share of raw-material cost, FY26

blocks.text: Concentration sits with suppliers, not customers. A Chinese supply disruption or price spike in technicals would hit both availability and gross margin. In-house technical capacity of 6,600 MTPA is small next to the 60,900 MT/KL formulation footprint (S9, S29).

The Frost & Sullivan report commissioned for the DRHP puts the Indian crop protection market at about USD 5.52 billion in FY25, up from USD 4.05 billion in FY20, and expects about USD 8.5 billion by FY30 (S7). That works out to roughly 6.4% a year historically and roughly 9% a year projected (our arithmetic from S7's figures). The global agrochemicals market is far larger but growing more slowly, at a projected 3.4% CAGR for 2024-2030 per one industry estimate (S19).

The Indian market is structurally difficult. FMC's own explanation for exiting its India commercial business cited a fragmented distribution channel, intense generic competition, complex regulation, high working-capital needs and challenging pricing. It also noted that generics of its insecticide Rynaxypyr spread faster than expected after the patent expired (S12). Crystal is buying into exactly that environment.
Demand depends on monsoon rainfall, cropping patterns and pest pressure, which makes revenue lumpy by season and year (S1, S14).

The offer documents name Kaveri Seed, Sumitomo Chemical India, Bayer CropScience, Rallis India and Dhanuka Agritech as listed peers (S20). Review coverage adds UPL, PI Industries, Bharat Rasayan, Heranba and Insecticides India to the competitive set (S20). Crystal also competes with many unlisted generic formulators. Through FMC India it is acquiring a former multinational competitor's local business (S12, S13).

blocks.caption: Return on net worth versus peers (FY25, per peer comparison in offer-document summaries; returns only, no valuation)

blocks.text: Crystal's returns resemble Rallis's, not those of the high-return branded players. The best peers earn about three times Crystal's return on equity from a similar product category, which suggests Crystal's scale has not yet produced pricing power (S20).

Plainly, no hard moat. Crystal holds 583 domestic registrations across 23 states and three union territories, plus 78 international registrations in 19 jurisdictions (S10). Registrations cost time and money, but every serious peer holds them. No source claims Crystal is the only or first Indian maker of any molecule. The company's regulatory page makes no first-to-register claim (S10). Most of the portfolio is off-patent generics sold under brands (S8).

items: Real but replicable advantages: a distributor network of about 14,700, up 64% in two years (S1). Acquired brands and registrations, including Bayer's 'Sunrice' ethoxysulfuron herbicide (its 13th acquisition) and Bayer's hybrid seed lines (S25). A licence to FMC brands and preferred FMC pipeline access once that deal closes (S12).
Partial backward integration: about 18 technicals reportedly made in-house (S29), but about 42% of raw-material cost still comes from China (S29).
The 'innovation rate' was 19.56% of FY26 revenue (S1). This is a company-defined KPI, not evidence of proprietary molecules.

blocks.text: The competitive position rests on distribution reach and acquired brands. Those are assets, not barriers, and the gap to peer returns shows they have not yet produced pricing power.

Sources: revenue from operations S1, S6 and S4 (Q1). Total income, EBITDA and PAT S2, S5 and S6. Margins S1 and S6. FY25 EBITDA margin and PAT margins are our arithmetic. FY26 revenue rose 17.2% and PAT 22.4%. EBITDA rose 44.7% (S1, S6). The gap between EBITDA and PAT growth comes from higher finance costs, depreciation and amortisation of acquired intangibles, which SMC Global flags as a recurring non-cash charge (S5, S14).
Q1 is the peak quarter: kharif seed and agrochemical sales are front-loaded. Q1 FY27 PAT of Rs.135.78 cr is almost the whole of FY26's Rs.144.91 cr, and should not be annualised (S5).

subsections.title: Balance sheet, debt and working capital

blocks.text: Sources: S2 and S5, with ratios from S2. Borrowings jumped 64% in FY25, the year of the I&B Seeds acquisition. They eased in FY26 and then rose about 16% in the June 2026 quarter (S5, S11). Fund-based borrowings were Rs.962.6 cr by August 2026 (S4). Net worth rose about Rs.440 cr in FY26, about Rs.295 cr more than that year's profit. This implies equity was raised during the year. We could not verify the exact equity history from the RHP.

Working capital is the core financial issue. Inventory days rose from 122 in FY24 to 160 in FY26. Receivable days fell from 95 to 70 (S23). Net working-capital days were reported at 139 in FY26, with inventory of Rs.1,379.07 cr (S23). A 2018 CRISIL rationale had already described the business as working-capital heavy, with gross current assets at about 255 days (S24).

blocks.caption: Operating cash flow vs PAT (Rs. crore)
rows: Cash flow from operations (B.N. Rathi note)

blocks.text: Over three years, operating cash flow has exceeded reported profit, which is reassuring. Cash flow did fall about a third in FY26 even as EBITDA rose 45%, because inventory built up (S23). Secondary sources disagree on the exact figures: Trendlyne shows about Rs.244 cr for FY26, and Finology showed about Rs.276 cr and Rs.348 cr for FY24 and FY25. The RHP cash-flow statement should be the tie-breaker. We could not read it directly (S23).

Verdict on the numbers: growth and margin expansion are real. But returns are still single-digit on equity, profit lags EBITDA, and growth is absorbing cash into inventory. The trend supports a 'getting better' story, not a 'high-quality compounder' story.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Issue at a glance
rows: 37,02,694 shares, ~Rs.100.71 cr, by promoter Ankur Aggarwal
Open 18 Nov; close 20 Nov; allotment 23 Nov; listing 26 Nov 2026 (BSE, NSE)
QIB not more than 50%, NII not less than 15%, retail not less than 35%
IIFL Capital, DAM Capital, Motilal Oswal / MUFG Intime

blocks.text: The issue has shrunk since the December 2025 DRHP. That filing proposed a Rs.600 cr fresh issue plus an OFS of 74.05 lakh shares, with IFC and IFC Emerging Asia Fund among the sellers (S7). The fresh issue was cut to Rs.439.2 cr and then to Rs.355 cr after a pre-IPO placement of Rs.84.29 cr at Rs.272.07 a share. The OFS was halved, and IFC dropped out as a seller (S4). IFC still holds 8.29%, and WhiteOak holds 1.03% after the pre-IPO round (S4).

blocks.caption: Use of fresh-issue proceeds (Rs. crore)
rows: Repayment/prepayment of certain borrowings of the company
Investment in material subsidiary Saffire Crop Science for its debt repayment
Unidentified acquisitions, strategic initiatives and general corporate purposes
Balance (~84.77 before issue expenses); capped at 35% of gross proceeds
Offer for sale (to promoter, not the company)

blocks.text: About three-quarters of the fresh money retires debt. That cuts interest cost from about Rs.962.6 cr of fund-based borrowings (S4). But the debt is largely seasonal working-capital funding that rebuilds every kharif season: borrowings rose from Rs.820 cr to Rs.952 cr in the June 2026 quarter alone (S6). None of the proceeds funds capacity, R&D or the FMC India purchase specifically (S2, S11).

The $252 million FMC India acquisition, cleared by the CCI and expected to close by end-2026, is many times the size of this fresh issue. The sources reviewed do not disclose how it will be paid for. One commentary describes it as a Rs.2,268 cr unfunded acquisition. More debt or another equity raise is a real possibility for post-IPO shareholders (S13, S26, S28).
The OFS of about Rs.100.71 cr goes entirely to promoter Ankur Aggarwal (S1). It is modest relative to the promoter group's 84.92% stake (S2), so it does not signal a promoter exit.

The promoters are Nand Kishore Aggarwal, his son Ankur Aggarwal, Komal Aggarwal and the Ankur Aggarwal KNK Family Trust (S2). Nand Kishore Aggarwal founded the group and led it for about four decades. In November 2025 he became Chairman Emeritus, and Ankur Aggarwal, previously Managing Director, became Executive Chairman and MD (S18). Both have been directors since at least August 2011, per corporate registry data (S27). At IFC's 2021-22 entry, the family held 94.7% and an employee welfare trust 5.3% (S8).

The track record is one of a long-tenured family operator that grows by acquisition. Crystal had made 13 acquisitions by January 2025, including Bayer's hybrid seed and ethoxysulfuron businesses, then I&B Seeds and now FMC India (S1, S25). The family also has history with capital markets. Crystal filed for a Rs.1,000 cr IPO in 2018 and got SEBI approval but never launched it (S7). It has since taken institutional money from IFC, with USD 14.91 million in equity invested in 2022 (S8).

items: Board: corporate registry data shows eight directors (S27).

Independent director Chetan Rameshchandra Desai was reportedly fined Rs.0.50 million and barred from audit work for five years by NFRA. The RHP reportedly notes the order does not disqualify him as an independent director, and that he chairs the audit committee (S22).
Statutory auditor: Walker Chandiok & Co LLP (S22).

blocks.text: The main disclosed related-party flow is with Aviral Crop Science Private Limited. It was paid Rs.65.82 cr in FY25 for field assistant expenses, about 2.45% of revenue from operations (S11). Ankur Aggarwal is a director of Aviral Crop Science (S27). That means part of the company's field force cost passes through a promoter-linked entity. The amount is large enough to matter and the arrangement is unusual. The arm's-length basis and FY26 figure could not be confirmed from the RHP directly. The FY25 figure comes from DRHP-based summaries (S11).

The RHP's risk factors state that the company has entered into related-party transactions and may continue to (S30). Beyond Aviral, the sources reviewed showed no promoter-linked suppliers of raw materials, promoter loans or unusual guarantees. Saffire Crop Science, which receives Rs.22.06 cr of the proceeds, is a subsidiary, not a promoter entity (S11).
This RPT section is not just routine. Paying about Rs.66 cr a year through a promoter-directed company for field staff is a structure investors should want explained and benchmarked.

In January 2020 the CBI filed a case against the company, two promoters and one director over alleged violations of the 2009-2014 Foreign Trade Policy, involving DFIA licences and Terminal Excise Duty refunds (S11, S17). The Additional DGFT, Ahmedabad, has raised a TED refund demand of Rs.109.42 cr plus interest, relating to refunds claimed in 2012-2016. The Gujarat High Court stayed the show-cause proceedings in December 2019 (S16). The ED has opened a PMLA investigation and provisionally attached Rs.30.21 cr of fixed deposits as of 31 March 2025 (S16). The company has filed discharge applications, and the RHP reportedly warns that outcomes are uncertain and further attachments are possible (S22).

blocks.caption: Audit and legal flags
rows: Rs.109.42 cr + interest; qualified opinion FY23 and FY24, emphasis of matter later
Rs.16.30 cr claim rejected by insurer, still booked. Qualified in FY22 and in the Sep-2025 interim accounts
Material weakness reported for FY23, FY24, FY25

blocks.text: This is not boilerplate. Criminal proceedings name the promoters themselves. The auditor has repeatedly qualified the accounts, and the audit committee chair reportedly carries an NFRA debarment. Taken together, governance is the weakest part of this investment case.

items: CBI/ED proceedings against the company and promoters: possible further attachments, penalties on the Rs.109.42 cr TED demand, and reputational damage with institutional investors (S16, S22).

FMC India funding and integration: a $252 million acquisition of a business its seller described as producing very limited EBITDA and needing heavy working capital. The funding is undisclosed and post-close leverage could rise sharply (S12, S26, S28).
China dependence: about 42% of FY26 raw-material cost, rising to about 49% in Q1 FY27. Historically one Chinese supplier provided over a quarter of purchases (S11, S29).
Monsoon and India concentration: 97.48% of revenue is domestic. A poor monsoon or pest year hits nearly the whole business, and seasonal working capital spikes debt every Q1 (S6, S11).
Working capital and cash conversion: 160 inventory days and up to 180-day distributor credit on some products. Operating cash flow fell in FY26 despite higher EBITDA (S23, S29).
Accounting and control quality: repeated audit qualifications and material weaknesses mean reported numbers carry more uncertainty than usual (S16).
Unallocated proceeds: up to 35% of gross proceeds may go to unidentified acquisitions and general purposes, giving management wide discretion (S11).

blocks.text: We have deliberately left out generic risks such as 'competition', 'key personnel' and 'regulatory changes' that every agrochemical prospectus carries.

blocks.caption: How each risk bears on the call
rows: High: governance and possible cash outflow
High: deal expected to close by end-2026
High: could undo the IPO deleveraging
Medium: keeps ROE in single digits

blocks.text: Likelihood and impact are our judgement, based on the cited facts above (S6, S12, S16, S29). Two of the top risks are governance and the pending acquisition. Neither can be judged from historical financials, which is why we don't think the numbers alone justify applying at IPO.

Management's concrete forward statements in the sources reviewed centre on the FMC India deal. Ankur Aggarwal said Crystal aims to 'accelerate innovation across both chemical and biological crop protection' and to welcome FMC India's workforce (S12). The deal gives Crystal FMC's India brands under licence, a preferred supply agreement for selected FMC active ingredients and formulations, and preferred access to FMC's active-ingredient pipeline for India, while FMC keeps its global R&D and manufacturing in India (S12, S26). The CCI approved it around early October 2026, after a long-form review over overlapping businesses (S13).

items: The November 2025 leadership transition was framed as preparing for a 'next phase of growth, innovation and global relevance', but came with no numerical targets (S18).
Capex: a greenfield formulation-plus-technical plant at Jhagadia, Gujarat, with about Rs.100 cr over three years (S31).

In-house technicals: IFC's 2022 investment was explicitly to expand in-house active-ingredient manufacturing and reduce import dependence. China's still-high share (~42%) shows that progress has been gradual (S8, S29).

blocks.text: We found no specific revenue or margin guidance in the RHP summaries or recent interviews. Older press reports of 15-20% growth ambitions predate the current filing and are not treated as guidance here. Any outlook beyond the FMC integration would be our inference from history, not something management has committed to.

Near term, three things matter. The first is the 2026-27 rabi and 2027 kharif seasons, because demand is weather-driven (S1). The second is how FMC India's brands are absorbed and financed (S12). The third is whether working capital stays at the FY26 level of about 139 net days or improves (S23). Sell-side IPO notes are mostly 'subscribe', citing the integrated model and debt reduction. SBI Securities is a notable exception, preferring to wait a few quarters after listing and citing monsoon dependence and modest return ratios (S14).

Upside comes from margin gains continuing, as in FY24-26 when EBITDA margin rose from 9.38% to 14.47% (S1), and from FMC's molecules adding pricing power the generic portfolio lacks. Downside comes from leverage after the FMC deal and any adverse step in the CBI/ED matters (S16, S22).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and GMP

blocks.text: On 17 November 2026 the company raised Rs.135.96 cr from 17 anchor investors, allotting 49,98,708 shares at Rs.272, the top of the band (S2, S14). By category, FPIs took Rs.60.65 cr (44.61%), mutual funds Rs.60.21 cr (44.28%), NBFCs Rs.10.00 cr and AIFs Rs.5.11 cr (S2). Named anchors include IFC, Nomura Singapore, Citigroup Global Markets Mauritius, WhiteOak MF, Tata MF, Groww MF and Ashoka India Equity Investment Trust (S14, S15). Lock-in: 50% of anchor shares until 23 December 2026 and the rest until 21 February 2027 (S2).
IFC is already an 8.29% shareholder and was in the anchor book. An existing investor anchoring is not independent price discovery (S4, S15).

Day-1 subscription by category (QIB/NII/retail) was not published at the time of writing. Upstox's 09:37 IST update said figures would appear after 10 am. A live tracker showed 0x, which reflects a pre-bid snapshot, not demand (S15, S32). Any reading of demand has to wait for the exchange data through 20 November.

Grey market premium (unofficial, not an investment signal): one tracker reported Rs.45 on 13 November (S32). Business Today reported Rs.18-20 on 18 November (S14). The fall and the disagreement between sources are themselves reasons not to rely on GMP.

sources.title: Crystal Crop Protection IPO GMP Today; Subscription Status Live

method: Researched on 2026-11-18, the issue's opening day. Two primary filings exist but could not be read in full: the SEBI-hosted offer document (S21) came back as compressed binary that could not be extracted, and the lead manager's RHP PDF (S22) was too large to download. Local PDF tools were not available. Material figures were therefore built from secondary summaries of the RHP and DRHP and cross-checked across at least two sources where possible. The restated P&L and balance sheet (total income, EBITDA, PAT, borrowings, assets) match across Chittorgarh, Chanakya Nipothi, IPO Guru and Multibagg (S2, S5, S6, S11). Revenue from operations and margins come from IPO Ji and Multibagg (S1, S6). The objects of the issue match across S1, S2, S3 and S11. Governance items (CBI/ED, TED demand, audit qualifications) were cross-checked across S11, S16 and S17. Several items rest on search-result excerpts only, from pages that blocked direct fetching: the NFRA order on the audit committee chair (S22), cash-flow and working-capital days (S23), China raw-material share and FY26 top-10 supplier share (S29), and the Rs.2,268 cr FMC funding characterisation and Q1 FY27 supplier figures (S28). Treat these as less certain. Operating cash flow figures differ between sources and are flagged in the text. FY26 related-party amounts, plant-wise capacity utilisation and FMC India's own revenue could not be confirmed. FY25 EBITDA margin, PAT margins and market CAGRs are our own arithmetic. As instructed, valuation is excluded: no P/E, EV/EBITDA or peer multiples, and the market-cap and multiple figures some sources volunteered were left out. Day-1 subscription data was not yet published at the time of writing. GMP is reported only as unofficial context.
